separating-mixtures-s1.title: Identifying the dyes in a drink
separating-mixtures-s1.text: A student spots a sports drink and four known food dyes on one strip of chromatography paper and develops it with a salt-water solvent. The solvent front ends 8.0 cm above the start line.

table.caption: Spot positions above the start line

separating-mixtures-s2.title: Distilling a mixture of two liquids
separating-mixtures-s2.text: A student distills a mixture of two liquids, acetone and water, and records the temperature of the vapor at the top of the apparatus as liquid collects in the receiving flask.

items.q: What is the Rf of the drink's higher spot?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the solvent distance by the spot distance. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, so it is never above 1.

why.correct: Rf = 6.4 cm ÷ 8.0 cm = 0.80. The distances share units, so Rf has none.

items.q: Which dyes are present in the drink? Select all that apply.
options: Dye A
Dye B
Dye C
Dye D

why.correct: The drink's spots have Rf = 6.4/8.0 = 0.80 and 2.0/8.0 = 0.25, matching Dye A (0.80) and Dye C (0.25).
options: Right: Rf 0.80 matches.
Dye B has Rf 0.50; the drink has no spot there.
Right: Rf 0.25 matches.
Dye D has Rf 0.15; the drink has no spot there.

items.q: Dye D has the smallest Rf. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Dye D is held most strongly by the paper relative to the solvent.
Dye D has the most mass, so it is too heavy to be carried far up the paper.
Dye D interacts most strongly with the solvent, so it stays near the start line.
Dye D was spotted last, so it had the least time to travel up the paper.

why.correct: A small Rf means the component spent most of its time attached to the stationary phase. That reflects stronger attractions to the paper than to the solvent.
options: Right: held most by the stationary phase.
Separation follows attractions to the two phases, not mass.
Strong attraction to the solvent would carry it farther, giving a large Rf.
All samples develop together for the same time.

items.q: The student marked the start line in ink instead of pencil. How might this affect the results?
options: The ink could separate into its own spots and be mistaken for dyes in the drink.
The ink line would block the solvent from rising, so the spots would stay on the start line.
There is no effect, because the ink line is below the spots and is not part of the samples.
Each Rf would double, because the ink adds its own distance to each measured spot distance.

why.correct: Ink is itself a mixture of dyes and would travel with the solvent, producing spots that could be mistaken for parts of the drink. Pencil (graphite) does not move.
options: Right: the line's own dyes would separate.
Solvent crosses an ink line easily.
The ink line is in the solvent's path and would move with it.
Rf uses measured distances; ink does not change them systematically.

items.q: The experiment is repeated with a much less polar solvent. What would most likely happen to the Rf values of these polar food dyes?
options: They would decrease, because the dyes would be held more by the polar paper.
They would increase, because a less polar solvent moves faster up the paper and carries the dyes.
They would stay the same, because Rf depends on the dye and not on the solvent used.
They would rise to about 1.00, because the dyes would move with the solvent front.

why.correct: Polar dyes are attracted to the polar paper. A less polar solvent attracts them less, so they spend more time on the paper and travel a smaller fraction of the solvent distance.
options: Right: less competition from the solvent, smaller Rf.
Rf is a ratio, so speed does not raise it; attractions decide.
Rf depends on the pair of phases; changing the solvent changes it.
Polar dyes would be held back, not swept to the front.
Water, which boils at about 100 °C
Acetone, which boils at about 56 °C
Both at once, in equal amounts
Neither, until 100 °C is reached

why.correct: The vapor stays near 56–61 °C for the first 30 mL: that is acetone, the lower-boiling liquid, vaporizing first.
options: Water comes over later, at the 100 °C plateau.
Right: the first plateau is near acetone's boiling point.
The two plateaus show they come over one after the other.
Liquid starts collecting at 56 °C.

items.q: Which statement best explains why acetone distills first?
options: Acetone has weaker intermolecular forces, so its vapor pressure is higher.
Acetone molecules are heavier than water molecules, so they rise into the vapor first.
Water molecules break apart at 56 °C, so they stay behind in the boiling flask.
Acetone hydrogen-bonds more strongly than water, so it leaves the liquid together.

why.correct: Acetone has dipole-dipole and dispersion forces but cannot hydrogen-bond to itself; water hydrogen-bonds extensively. Weaker attractions give acetone the higher vapor pressure and the lower boiling point.
options: Right: weaker attractions, more volatile.
Heavier molecules would not escape more easily; and attractions, not mass, decide.
Water molecules stay intact; no covalent bonds break.
Acetone has no H bonded to O, so it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself.

items.q: About how much acetone was in the original mixture?
options: About 10 mL
About 30 mL
About 60 mL
About 100 mL

why.correct: The vapor stays near acetone's boiling point until about 30 mL have collected, then the temperature rises sharply toward 100 °C as water starts to come over.
options: Liquid at acetone's temperature kept collecting past 10 mL.
Right: the first plateau ends near 30 mL.
60 mL is the total collected, including water.
The table shows only 60 mL collected.

items.q: The 35 mL sample, collected at 78 °C, is tested. What is it most likely to be?
options: A mixture of both, since 78 °C lies between their boiling points.
Pure acetone, since the liquid collected below 100 °C is acetone.
Pure water, since water starts to boil once the temperature passes 61 °C.
A new compound, formed when acetone and water reacted during heating.

why.correct: Between the plateaus, both liquids are vaporizing in a changing ratio, so the distillate is a mixture. A simple distillation does not cut perfectly between two liquids.
options: Right: the transition region holds both.
At 78 °C, well above acetone's boiling point, water is coming over too.
Water vaporizes at every temperature; at 78 °C both liquids are in the vapor.
Distillation is a physical separation; no reaction occurs.

items.q: Which method separates sand from a mixture of sand and salt water?
options: Filtration
Chromatography
Distillation
Evaporating the water

why.correct: Sand has not dissolved, so its grains stay on filter paper while the salt water passes through.
options: Right: undissolved solid from a liquid.
Chromatography separates dissolved components, not a coarse solid.
Distillation would leave both sand and salt behind together.
Evaporation would leave salt mixed with the sand.

items.q: Why does filtration not separate the salt from salt water?
options: Dissolved ions are far smaller than the pores of the paper.
Salt ions stick to the filter paper and block it before any water passes.
Filtration works on gases, not on liquids such as salt water.
The salt reacts with the paper and forms a new dissolved compound.

why.correct: A solution is mixed down to individual particles. Ions are about 10⁻¹⁰ m across, thousands of times smaller than filter pores, so they pass through with the water.
options: Right: dissolved particles pass through.
The ions pass through freely; they do not clog the filter.
Filtration is used for liquids all the time.
No reaction occurs with filter paper.

items.q: Which method would best recover pure water from seawater?
options: Distillation, because water vaporizes while the ions stay behind.
Filtration, because the ions are trapped by the filter paper.
Chromatography, because the salt moves faster than the water.
Decanting, because the salt settles to the bottom over time.

why.correct: Water has a measurable vapor pressure; the ions, held by strong ion-dipole and ionic attractions, do not enter the vapor. Condensing the vapor gives pure water.
options: Right: water vaporizes, ions stay behind.
Ions pass through filter paper.
Chromatography separates small samples of dissolved components; it does not yield pure water in bulk.
Dissolved salt does not settle out of a solution.

items.q: Hexane (C₆H₁₄) and 1-propanol (C₃H₇OH) are separated on a column packed with polar silica (covered in –OH groups) using a nonpolar solvent. Which comes out of the column first, and why?
options: Hexane, because it is barely attracted to the polar silica.
1-Propanol, because it hydrogen-bonds to the solvent and is carried along.
Hexane, because it is the heavier molecule and falls through the column faster.
1-Propanol, because it has fewer carbon atoms and fits through the packing.

why.correct: The polar silica holds 1-propanol by hydrogen bonds; nonpolar hexane interacts only weakly with it and stays in the mobile phase, so it leaves first.
options: Right: weakest attraction to the stationary phase moves fastest.
A nonpolar solvent cannot hydrogen-bond; 1-propanol is held by the silica instead.
Separation follows attractions, not falling speed.
Size is not the main factor here; polarity is.

items.q: On a chromatogram, the solvent front is 12.5 cm from the start line and a spot is 4.0 cm from it. What is the spot's Rf?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, which is at most 1.

why.correct: Rf = 4.0 cm ÷ 12.5 cm = 0.32 (two significant figures, from 4.0).

items.q: Which differences in physical properties are used to separate mixtures? Select all that apply.
options: Particle size (filtration)
Attraction to a stationary phase (chromatography)
Vapor pressure (distillation)
Number of protons in the nucleus
Molar mass alone (heavier parts left behind)
Total mass of the sample

why.correct: Each physical method exploits a property that differs between components. The number of protons defines an element; physical separations do not change or use it.
options: Right: larger particles stay on the filter.
Right: stronger attraction to the stationary phase slows a component.
Right: the more volatile component vaporizes first.
Protons identify elements; physical separations neither use nor change them.
Separations follow attractions and size, not molar mass by itself.
The total mass says nothing about the parts of the mixture.

items.q: Put the steps for running a paper chromatogram in order.
options: Draw a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper
Place a small spot of each sample on the line
Stand the paper in solvent below the start line
Remove the paper when the solvent is near the top and mark the solvent front
Measure the distances and calculate each Rf

why.correct: The start line must sit above the solvent so the spots are not washed off, and the solvent front must be marked before it evaporates.
